question: A 35-year-old African American man presents with fever, abdominal pain, and severe weakness since yesterday. On physical examination, the patient is jaundiced and shows a generalized pallor. Past medical history is significant for recently receiving anti-malaria prophylaxis before visiting Nigeria. Laboratory tests show normal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) levels. Peripheral smear shows the presence of bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fever and abdominal pain" -> "Jaundice and pallor" -> "Bite cells and Heinz bodies on smear" -> "Recent anti-malaria prophylaxis" -> "G6PD deficiency suspected" -> "Normal G6PD levels" -> "Unclear diagnosis" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Fever and abdominal pain" -> "Jaundice and pallor" -> "Bite cells and Heinz bodies on smear" -> "Recent anti-malaria prophylaxis" -> "G6PD deficiency suspected" -> "Normal G6PD levels" -> "Possible drug-induced hemolytic anemia" -> 70%

analysis: The patient's symptoms and laboratory findings are indicative of hemolytic anemia. The presence of bite cells and Heinz bodies on the peripheral smear is characteristic of oxidative damage to red blood cells, which is commonly seen in Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Although the laboratory tests show normal G6PD levels, it is important to note that testing during an acute hemolytic episode can yield false-normal results due to the destruction of older, more enzyme-deficient red blood cells. The recent use of anti-malaria prophylaxis, which can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, supports this diagnosis. Therefore, despite the normal G6PD levels, the clinical presentation and peripheral smear findings strongly suggest G6PD deficiency.
